summary: Specifies the Host Monitoring Protocol, used to collect information from various kinds of hosts in the Internet. Designers of communications software were encouraged to consider it for monitoring their systems. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 869 defines HMP, a simple transport protocol for monitoring machines across the Internet. One machine, the monitoring centre, asks the other for information by sending a poll; the monitored machine replies with the data it has collected. The protocol handles three kinds of data: events that happen spontaneously, the current state of the machine, and counters gathered over time.

questions: what is the host monitoring protocol
subtitle: A transport protocol in which one machine polls another for measurements and status.

tldr.problem: Networks needed a way to collect measurements and status from the machines on them, including machines of several different kinds, and to do it without putting the intelligence for monitoring inside every host.
tldr.mechanism: HMP puts the intelligence in the monitoring centre. The centre asks a host for a particular kind of data with a poll, and the host replies with the data it has collected; if a poll or a reply is lost, the centre polls again. Traps report events as they happen, and statistics are collected over an interval and sent when polled.
tldr.outcome: RFC 869 is Historic and the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It replaced the earlier document IEN-197 of the same name, and the memo says it was being used with Internet gateways and TACs, with implementations being designed for other kinds of host.

sections.title: What HMP Is For
sections.content:
The Host Monitoring Protocol is used to collect information from hosts in various networks. A host is defined as an addressable Internet entity that can send and receive messages, which includes server hosts, personal workstations, terminal concentrators, packet switches and gateways. At present the protocol was being used to collect information from Internet gateways and TACs, and implementations were being designed for other hosts. It is designed to monitor hosts spread over the Internet as well as hosts in a single network.

The document is organised in three parts. Sections 2 and 3 give a general description of the protocol and its relationship to other protocols. Section 4 describes how it operates. Sections 5 and 6 describe the HMP messages and their formats. These are followed by appendices containing the formats of messages sent by some of the hosts that use HMP to collect their monitoring information; those appendices are included as examples only and are not part of the protocol.

This document replaces the previous HMP document, IEN-197, A Host Monitoring Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Any machine on the network that can send and receive messages counts as a host for this purpose, whether it is a server, a workstation, a terminal concentrator or a router. The protocol was in use with routers and terminal concentrators at the time of writing. The appendices at the end show the specific messages those machines sent, as examples rather than as part of the protocol itself.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Interaction
sections.content:
HMP is a transaction-oriented, connectionless transport protocol, designed to facilitate certain simple interactions between two Internet entities, one of which may be considered to be monitoring the other. The discussion speaks of a monitoring host and a monitored entity. HMP was intended to be useful for applications involving any or all of three kinds of interaction.

First, the monitored entity sometimes needs to send unsolicited datagrams to the monitoring host. The monitoring host should be able to tell when messages from the monitored entity have been lost in transit, and be able to determine the order in which the messages were sent, but the application does not require that all messages be received or that they be received strictly in the same sequence in which they were sent.

Second, the monitoring host needs to gather data from the monitored entity by using a query-response protocol at the application level. It must be able to determine which query is being answered by a particular response, and to determine whether successive responses are duplicates of previous ones.

Third, the monitoring host must be able to initiate certain control functions in the monitored entity, possibly including the setting of parameters in it, and needs to know if the control function has been carried out.

The design also assumes that a given monitoring host may be monitoring several different types of entities at the same time, and may be gathering several different types of data from a given type of entity, and that several monitoring hosts may be monitoring a given entity, and several processes on the same host may even be monitoring the same entity.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things have to work. Events that happen on their own have to reach the monitoring centre, and the centre must be able to see that some were lost and put the rest in order. Requests for measurements have to be matched to their answers, so the centre can tell a fresh answer from a repeat. And the centre must be able to change settings on the machine and know whether the change happened. Several centres may watch the same machine at once, and one centre may watch several kinds of machine.

sections.title: Where HMP Sits in the Protocol Stack
sections.content:
HMP is a transport protocol designed to fit into the layered Internet protocol environment. It operates on top of the Internet and ICMP protocol and under applications that require its services. The diagram in the memo places the applications, TELNET, FTP, GATEWAY and TAC, in the application layer; TCP and HMP in the transport layer; the Internet Protocol and ICMP in the internetwork layer; and the local network protocol in the network layer.

If internetwork services are not required it should be possible to run HMP without an internetwork layer. As long as HMP's service requirements, addressing, protocol demultiplexing and occasional delivery, are met, it should run over a variety of protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: HMP sits where TCP sits: between the application and IP. It carries the monitoring messages and offers the same kind of service, so an application written for it could in principle run over TCP instead. The memo also notes that if the network below does not provide internetwork services, HMP could still run as long as addressing, telling different protocols apart, and the occasional delivery of a message are available.

sections.title: Polling, Traps and Statistics
sections.content:
The protocol is built around the idea that most of the intelligence needed to monitor a host should reside in a monitoring centre, not in the host. The host should be required only to collect data and send it to the monitoring centre, either spontaneously or on request. The host is not responsible for ensuring that the data arrives reliably, except that it checksums the data; instead the monitoring centre is responsible for ensuring that the data it requests is received correctly.

HMP is therefore based on polling hosts for messages. When the monitoring centre requires a particular type of data, such as throughput data, it sends a poll to the host requesting that type of report. The host responds with its latest set of collected data. If the host finds that the poll is incorrect, for example a poll for throughput data when the host is not collecting throughput data, it responds with an error message. The monitoring centre waits a reasonable length of time for the host to answer, and if no response is received it sends another poll for the same data. In this way, if either a poll or the response is lost, the correct data is still collected.

The protocol collects three classes of data. Spontaneous events, or traps, report events as they occur, and to insure their prompt delivery are sent as datagrams with no reliability mechanisms such as acknowledgments and retransmissions, except checksums. A trap usually contains an identifier saying which event is being reported, the local time in the host at which the event occurred, and data pertinent to the event, the content of which is host and event specific.

Status information describes the current state of the host. It is useful at one point and does not have to be collected cumulatively over a period, so only the latest status is of interest and old status provides no useful information. The monitoring centre collects it by sending a poll for status, and the host always creates a new status message when it answers. If no response arrives, the centre polls again, and it can decide whether the host is up or down based on whether it responds.

Statistical data are measurements taken over time, such as the number of packets sent or received by a host and the count of packets dropped for a particular reason. It is important that none of this data be lost. It is collected in the host over a time interval; when the interval expires the current data is copied to another area and the counters are cleared. The copied data is sent to the monitoring centre when the host receives a poll requesting statistical information, and if another poll arrives before the interval has expired the data in the buffer is sent again. The monitoring centre can detect duplicate messages using the sequence number in the header, since each type of statistical data has its own sequence number counter. The collection frequency for statistics messages from a particular host must be relatively long compared to the average round trip message time, to allow the centre to re-poll. Each statistics message contains a field giving the local time when the data was collected and the time at which the message was sent, which allows the centre to schedule its poll so that it arrives near the beginning of each collection period.

HMP also provides for sending data to and reading parameters in hosts. The data may set switches or interval timers used to control measurements, or control the host itself, such as a restart switch, and the format of the data and parameters is host specific. To send data, the monitoring centre sends a poll for a control acknowledgment message, which includes the type of the data and the data being sent; the host processes it and responds with a control acknowledgment. To read parameters, the centre sends a poll for parameters, including the type of parameters being read, and the host answers with a parameters message.
sections.plainLanguage: The monitoring centre does the thinking and the host does the measuring. The centre asks for a particular report, the host sends its latest figures, and if nothing comes back the centre asks again, so a lost message does not lose the data. Events that matter immediately are pushed out as traps, which are sent without any guarantee of arrival because speed matters more than completeness there. Counters are gathered over a fixed period, and the period is made long enough that the centre has time to ask again if a reply is lost.

sections.title: The HMP Header
sections.content:
An HMP message consists of local network headers, an IP header, the HMP header, the data area, and padding. The messages are sent using the version 4 IP header described in RFC 791. The HMP protocol number is 20 in decimal, and the time to live field should be set to a reasonable value for the hosts being monitored; all other fields should be set as specified in RFC 791.

The HMP header is five 16-bit words. The first word holds the system type and the message type, and their combination determines the format of the data in the monitoring message. The system types defined are 1 Monitoring Host, 2 IMP, 3 TAC, 4 Gateway, 5 SIMP, 6 BBN VAX/C70 TCP, 7 PAD, 8 Reserved, 9 TIU, 10 FEP, 11 Cronus Host and 12 Cronus MCS.

The message types are defined and used for each system type according to the needs of that system: 1 Trap, 2 Status, 3 Thruput, 4 HTM for the Host Traffic Matrix, 5 Parameters, 6 Routing, 7 Call Accounting, 100 Poll, 101 Error and 102 Control Acknowledgment.

The second word holds the port number and the control flag. The port number can be used to multiplex similar messages to and from different processes in one host, and is currently unused. The control flag passes control information, and currently bit 15 is defined as the More bit, used in a message in response to a poll to indicate that there is more data to poll for.

The third word is the sequence number, which is present in every message and is incremented when each new message of that type is sent. The fourth word is the password or the returned sequence number. In a polling message from a monitoring centre it holds a password to verify that the centre is allowed to gather information; responses to polling messages copy the sequence number from the polling message and return it in this field, for identification and round trip time calculations. The fifth word is the checksum, the one's complement of the one's complement sum of all the 16-bit words in the header and data area.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message carries a ten-byte header with five fields. The first says what kind of machine is talking and what kind of message it is, which together tell the receiver how to read the rest. The second carries a port number, reserved for telling several processes on one machine apart, and a control flag whose top bit says there is more to fetch. The third is a sequence number that counts messages of that type. The fourth is either a password, when the centre is polling, or the sequence number of the poll being answered. The fifth is a checksum over the header and the data.

sections.title: The Monitoring Centre's Messages
sections.content:
Three message types are defined for the monitoring centre itself. Message type 100 is the polling message. The monitoring centre sends polls to the hosts it monitors to collect their monitoring data; when the host receives a poll it returns a message of the type requested. It will only answer a poll with the correct system type and password, and will return an error message, type 101, if it receives a poll for the wrong system type or an unsupported message type.

The poll message includes a facility to send data to a monitored host: a poll for a control acknowledgment message, type 102, followed by the data, with the R-Subtype specifying the type of data being sent. When the monitored host receives such a poll it processes the data and then responds with a control acknowledgment message; if it cannot process the data it should respond with an error message. A poll to read parameters consists of a poll for a parameters message, with the R-Subtype specifying the type of parameters being read, and the host responds with a parameters message containing the requested information.

The poll message has an R-Message Type giving the message type requested and an R-Subtype used when sending data and reading parameters. When the poll is requesting a control acknowledgment message, data is included in the poll message; a poll for any other type of message does not include any data, and the contents of the data are host specific. The sequence number identifies the polling request, and the monitoring centre maintains separate sequence numbers for each host it monitors; the sequence number is returned in the response so the centre can associate polls with their responses and determine round trip times. The password field holds the monitoring password.

Message type 101, the error in poll message, is sent in response to a faulty poll and specifies the nature of the error. Its error type field has the values 1 reason unspecified, 2 bad R-Message Type, 3 bad R-Subtype, 4 unknown parameter, 5 invalid parameter value, 6 invalid parameter/value format and 7 machine in loader. The R-Message Type and R-Subtype fields identify the poll request in error, and the returned sequence number is the sequence number of the polling message which caused the error.

Message type 102, the control acknowledgment, is sent in response to a poll for this type of message and acknowledges poll messages used to set parameters in the monitored host. It has no fields other than the HMP header, and its returned sequence number is the sequence number of the polling message which requested it.
sections.plainLanguage: The centre sends polls, and the host answers with the type of message that was asked for. A poll names the message type it wants, and carries data only when it is asking the host to set something. If the poll is wrong, the host answers with an error message saying what was wrong: a bad message type, a bad subtype, an unknown parameter, an invalid value, a bad format, or that the machine is still loading. A separate acknowledgement message confirms that a setting was applied.

fields.name: System Type
fields.desc: The kind of machine: 1 Monitoring Host, 2 IMP, 3 TAC, 4 Gateway, and so on.

fields.name: Message Type
fields.desc: Trap, Status, Thruput, HTM, Parameters, Routing, Call Accounting, Poll, Error or Control Acknowledgment.

fields.name: Port Number
fields.desc: To multiplex messages between processes on one host. Currently unused.

fields.name: Control Flag
fields.desc: Bit 15 is the More bit, saying there is more data to poll for.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Incremented each time a new message of that type is sent.

fields.name: Password or Returned Sequence Number
fields.desc: A password in a poll, the poll's sequence number in a reply.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement of the one's complement sum of the header and data.

items.label: Poll
items.desc: Sent by the monitoring centre to ask for a report.

items.label: Error
items.desc: Sent by the host when a poll is faulty, with an error type.

items.label: Control Acknowledgment
items.desc: Confirms that data sent in a poll was applied.

items.label: Trap
items.desc: An unsolicited report of an event as it happens.

items.label: Status
items.desc: The current state of the machine.

items.label: Thruput
items.desc: Counters gathered over a collection period.

items.label: Parameters
items.desc: The parameters read back from the machine.

items.label: Routing
items.desc: The machine's interfaces, neighbours and routes.
